# The handoff deserves time of its own

After 24 years in county corrections, I’ve come to think that one of the most useful changes a facility can make is to set aside a few minutes for the shift handoff. I spent the early part of my career on the floor and later supervised shifts. At both levels, I saw how easily unfinished work could get lost when everyone assumed someone else had passed it along.

One ordinary example was a scheduled repair. The outgoing shift knew a shared room would be unavailable the next morning. The information was written down, but the incoming team had several updates to sort through and missed the timing. Staff found out when they tried to use the room and had to rearrange the morning schedule. A brief conversation would have given the incoming team a chance to check what was changing and who would follow up.

# What I’d cover

I’d ask the outgoing lead to say what changed, what still needs attention, and who owns the next step. The incoming lead should have a chance to ask a question or repeat back a deadline that could be misunderstood. The written log remains the place to record what was agreed, using the agency’s established rules for handling sensitive information.

In my experience, the conversation works best when it stays focused on what the next team needs to know. A long recap makes it harder to hear the one detail that matters. When the shift is busy, I’d start with the items that are time-sensitive and leave routine updates in the log.

# Start with one shift change

A supervisor could try this at one shift change for two weeks. At the end, ask both teams which details were easier to pass along and which still got missed. If the conversation regularly runs long, look at what staff are repeating from the log and shorten the spoken portion.

A handoff takes time, and staffing pressures are real. My view is that a short, scheduled exchange is worth trying because it gives both shifts a specific moment to check who will do what next. The people who use it every day should help decide what belongs in it.
